EU AI Act — Prototype Regulatory Corpus (Summary Form)
========================================================
NOTE: Plain-language summary for Policy RAG demo/retrieval purposes, not
verbatim legal text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Verified against current
public reporting as of August 2026; confirm against the official Official
Journal text and any further amendments before real use. This regulation's
timeline has already changed once via the Digital Omnibus (see below), so
treat every date in this document as subject to revision.

eu_ai_act_prototype::1.text:
Overview and phased timeline
----------------------------------------------------------------
The EU AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and applies obligations
in stages rather than all at once:
  - 2 February 2025: the Article 5 prohibited-practices regime became
    enforceable (certain social scoring, manipulative or exploitative
    systems, some biometric categorisation), alongside the Article 4 AI
    literacy duty requiring providers and deployers to ensure staff
    operating AI systems have a sufficient level of AI literacy.
  - 2 August 2025: obligations for providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI)
    models took effect.
  - 2 August 2026: Article 50 transparency obligations became enforceable
    -- disclosure that a user is interacting with an AI system, labelling
    of

eu_ai_act_prototype::2.text:
sparency obligations became enforceable
    -- disclosure that a user is interacting with an AI system, labelling
    of synthetic/deepfake content, and marking of AI-generated content.
    This date has already passed as of this document's writing and these
    obligations are now in effect and enforceable by national market
    surveillance authorities.
  - High-risk AI system obligations (Annex III: biometrics, critical
    infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law
    enforcement, migration, and administration of justice) were originally
    also scheduled for 2 August 2026. This has been formally deferred --
    see "Digital Omnibus" below, now enacted law rather than a pending
    proposal.

eu_ai_act_prototype::3.text:
nacted law rather than a pending
    proposal.

eu_ai_act_prototype::4.text:
Digital Omnibus on AI — now enacted, not merely proposed
----------------------------------------------------------------
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the "Digital Omnibus on AI," was published in
the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July
2026 -- six days before the AI Act's original 2 August 2026 high-risk
deadline. This is confirmed, enacted law, not a political agreement still
awaiting formal adoption. It defers standalone high-risk (Annex III)
obligations from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027, and high-risk AI
embedded in products already covered by separate EU product-safety law
(Annex I) to 2 August 2028. Three categories of obligation were
deliberately left untouched by this deferral and remain fully enforceable
on their original schedule: the Article 5 pr

eu_ai_act_prototype::5.text:
e
deliberately left untouched by this deferral and remain fully enforceable
on their original schedule: the Article 5 prohibited-practices regime
(since 2 February 2025), the Article 4 AI literacy duty (also since 2
February 2025), and the Article 50 transparency and content-labelling
obligations (since 2 August 2026, now in effect). GPAI provider
obligations under Article 53, in force since 2 August 2025, are likewise
unaffected. The Omnibus also introduced a narrow additional prohibited
practice into Article 5 covering AI-generated non-consensual intimate
imagery and child sexual abuse material. The overall architecture of the
Act -- its risk-based classification, conformity assessment regime, and
the AI Office's oversight role -- is unchanged; this is a timing
adjustment to the heaviest

eu_ai_act_prototype::6.text:
rmity assessment regime, and
the AI Office's oversight role -- is unchanged; this is a timing
adjustment to the heaviest compliance track, not a substantive rollback.

eu_ai_act_prototype::7.text:
The four-tier risk classification
----------------------------------------------------------------
The Act classifies AI systems into four risk tiers, and the obligations
that apply to a given system flow entirely from which tier it falls into:
unacceptable risk (Article 5 prohibited practices -- these systems may
not be placed on the market at all, regardless of context); high risk
(Annex III use-case list, or AI embedded in products already subject to
EU product-safety law under Annex I -- subject to the risk-management,
documentation, and human-oversight regime described below, now on the
deferred timeline); limited risk (primarily the Article 50 transparency
obligations -- chatbots, emotion-recognition systems, and synthetic-
content generators, which must disclose their AI nature but

eu_ai_act_prototype::8.text:
ns -- chatbots, emotion-recognition systems, and synthetic-
content generators, which must disclose their AI nature but face no
broader compliance regime); and minimal risk (the large majority of AI
applications, subject to no AI Act-specific obligations beyond voluntary
codes of conduct). Correctly classifying which tier a given AI use case
falls into is the foundational step every other AI Act obligation depends
on -- a governance system that already tags applications by criticality
and use case (loan-decision, hiring-decision, customer-support) is doing
work that maps directly onto this classification exercise, not a
separate one.

eu_ai_act_prototype::9.text:
High-risk obligations (Annex III) — deferred, not removed
----------------------------------------------------------------
Annex III lists the specific high-risk use-case categories: biometric
identification and categorisation; management of critical infrastructure;
education and vocational training (e.g. automated exam scoring or
admissions); employment, worker management, and access to self-employment
(e.g. automated CV screening or performance evaluation); access to
essential private and public services including credit scoring and
insurance risk assessment; law enforcement; migration, asylum, and border
control; and administration of justice and democratic processes. For
systems in these categories, the Act requires (once the deferred deadline
arrives): a risk-management system spannin

eu_ai_act_prototype::10.text:
For
systems in these categories, the Act requires (once the deferred deadline
arrives): a risk-management system spanning the AI system's lifecycle;
data governance measures for training/validation/testing data; technical
documentation and automatic logging capabilities; transparency
information for deployers; human oversight measures enabling a person to
understand the system's output and intervene or halt it; and defined
levels of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity. Employment decisions
and access to essential services are both explicitly listed categories --
this is the same reasoning ControlPlane already applies internally by
tagging loan-decision and hiring-decision applications as critical/
high-impact and routing them toward human review. That existing design
choice anticipates

eu_ai_act_prototype::11.text:
sion applications as critical/
high-impact and routing them toward human review. That existing design
choice anticipates the Annex III risk-management, human-oversight, and
logging obligations even though the hard legal deadline for those
specific obligations has moved out to December 2027 -- building toward it
now is schedule flexibility, not an excuse to stop.

eu_ai_act_prototype::12.text:
Article 14 — Human oversight
----------------------------------------------------------------
For high-risk systems, the Act requires human oversight measures
proportionate to the risks, appropriate to the context, and designed so
the overseeing person can: properly understand the system's capacities
and limitations, remain aware of "automation bias" (the tendency to
over-rely on automated output), correctly interpret the system's output,
decide not to use it or otherwise disregard, override, or reverse it in a
given instance, and intervene in or stop the system's operation. A
governance layer's HUMAN_REVIEW decision path, and its capture of what a
human reviewer actually decided when overriding a flagged output, is a
concrete operational instance of this obligation rather than an
independ

eu_ai_act_prototype::13.text:
decided when overriding a flagged output, is a
concrete operational instance of this obligation rather than an
independent design choice made for unrelated reasons.

eu_ai_act_prototype::14.text:
Article 50 — Transparency obligations (in force now)
----------------------------------------------------------------
Article 50 requires that providers ensure AI systems intended to interact
directly with natural persons are designed so those persons are informed
they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the
context to a reasonably well-informed person. It further requires
labelling of AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, or video content
that could appear to be authentic or truthful (synthetic/deepfake
content), and disclosure where text is AI-generated and published to
inform the public on matters of public interest, again with exceptions
where human review has taken place. This is already in force and
enforceable by national market surveillance authoritie

eu_ai_act_prototype::15.text:
where human review has taken place. This is already in force and
enforceable by national market surveillance authorities as of 2 August
2026, with penalties for non-compliance reaching up to EUR 15 million or
3% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. For a system like
ControlPlane, this means any user-facing AI interaction (e.g. the HR or
customer-support chatbot sitting behind the governance gateway) should be
clearly disclosed as AI-driven, and any synthetic content it produces
that could be mistaken for authentic material should be identifiable as
AI-generated -- an obligation that is live today, not a future
compliance project.

eu_ai_act_prototype::16.text:
Article 53 — Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models
----------------------------------------------------------------
Providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models -- the category most
foundation-model APIs an enterprise consumes fall into -- must maintain
technical documentation, provide information and documentation to
downstream providers integrating the model, put in place a policy to
respect EU copyright law, and publish a sufficiently detailed summary of
the content used to train the model. GPAI models classified as posing a
"systemic risk" (broadly, based on the compute used to train them) face
additional obligations: model evaluation, adversarial testing, tracking
and reporting serious incidents, and ensuring adequate cybersecurity
protection. These obligations sit w

eu_ai_act_prototype::17.text:
sting, tracking
and reporting serious incidents, and ensuring adequate cybersecurity
protection. These obligations sit with the model provider, not with an
enterprise consuming that model via API -- but an enterprise governance
layer benefits from knowing which GPAI provider and model version sits
behind each AI application it governs, since that provider's own
documentation and incident disclosures are relevant context for the
enterprise's own risk assessment of that application.

eu_ai_act_prototype::18.text:
Conformity assessment, documentation, and enforcement
----------------------------------------------------------------
High-risk AI systems must undergo a conformity assessment (self-assessed
for most Annex III categories, third-party assessed for a smaller subset)
before being placed on the market, and providers must register standalone
high-risk systems in an EU database. Article 99 sets out the Act's
general penalty structure: up to EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual
turnover for violations of the Article 5 prohibited-practices regime
(the most severe tier), up to EUR 15 million or 3% for most other
provider/deployer obligations including Article 50 transparency, and a
lower tier for supplying incorrect information to authorities. These
figures scale with company size for SMEs. Na

eu_ai_act_prototype::19.text:
and a
lower tier for supplying incorrect information to authorities. These
figures scale with company size for SMEs. National market surveillance
authorities and, for GPAI models, the EU AI Office, share enforcement
responsibility.

eu_ai_act_prototype::20.text:
What this corpus intentionally does not cover
----------------------------------------------------------------
This summary does not cover the detailed conformity assessment procedure
steps, CE marking mechanics, the specific technical documentation format
required under Annex IV, or the AI Office's evolving guidance documents
and codes of practice -- those are compliance-process specifics for
providers placing high-risk systems on the market, not directly relevant
to an internal governance control plane's retrieval corpus. Given the
regulation's demonstrated rate of amendment (one substantive deferral via
the Digital Omnibus within two years of entry into force), any date or
figure in this document should be re-verified against the current
Official Journal text before being relied on for

eu_ai_act_prototype::21.text:
e or
figure in this document should be re-verified against the current
Official Journal text before being relied on for an actual compliance
decision.

GDPR — Prototype Regulatory Corpus (Summary Form)
==================================================
NOTE ON THIS DOCUMENT: This is a prototype knowledge-base document for
ControlPlane.ai's Policy RAG. It is a plain-language SUMMARY of what each
article covers, written for retrieval and citation purposes in a demo
environment -- it is NOT the verbatim legal text of the Regulation, and
must not be used as a substitute for the official GDPR text (Regulation
(EU) 2016/679) or for legal advice. Replace with actual verified legal
source text (or a licensed regulatory database feed) before any real
compliance use.

gdpr_prototype::1.text:
Article 5 — Principles relating to processing of personal data
----------------------------------------------------------------
Article 5 sets out the core principles that govern all processing of
personal data under GDPR. Personal data must be: processed lawfully,
fairly, and transparently; collected for specified, explicit, and
legitimate purposes and not further processed in a way incompatible with
those purposes (purpose limitation); adequate, relevant, and limited to
what is necessary for those purposes (data minimisation); accurate and
kept up to date; kept in a form permitting identification of the data
subject for no longer than necessary (storage limitation); and processed
with appropriate security, integrity, and confidentiality. The controller
is responsible for, and must be abl

gdpr_prototype::2.text:
processed
with appropriate security, integrity, and confidentiality. The controller
is responsible for, and must be able to demonstrate compliance with,
these principles ("accountability"). For an enterprise AI governance
system, Article 5's data-minimisation and purpose-limitation principles
are directly relevant to any AI application that retrieves or surfaces
more personal data than the specific task requires.

gdpr_prototype::3.text:
Article 6 — Lawfulness of processing
----------------------------------------------------------------
Article 6 requires that processing of personal data have a valid legal
basis. It lists six possible bases: the data subject has given consent;
processing is necessary for performance of a contract with the data
subject; processing is necessary to comply with a legal obligation;
processing is necessary to protect the vital interests of the data
subject or another person; processing is necessary for a task carried out
in the public interest; or processing is necessary for the legitimate
interests of the controller or a third party, provided those interests
are not overridden by the data subject's rights and freedoms. An AI
system that accesses employee or customer personal data (for example,

gdpr_prototype::4.text:
n by the data subject's rights and freedoms. An AI
system that accesses employee or customer personal data (for example, an
HR copilot retrieving salary or leave records) must have an identifiable
Article 6 basis for that specific access, not merely a general basis for
holding the data in the first place.

gdpr_prototype::5.text:
Article 9 — Processing of special categories of personal data
----------------------------------------------------------------
Article 9 imposes a general prohibition on processing "special category"
personal data -- data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political
opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership,
genetic data, biometric data used for identification, health data, or
data concerning a person's sex life or sexual orientation. Processing
this category of data is prohibited unless one of the specific exceptions
in Article 9(2) applies (for example: explicit consent, employment/social
security law obligations, vital interests, or substantial public
interest with appropriate safeguards). Health data is squarely within
this special category, which is why an A

gdpr_prototype::6.text:
al public
interest with appropriate safeguards). Health data is squarely within
this special category, which is why an AI system that could surface
medical or health-adjacent information carries materially higher risk
than one handling ordinary personal data, and why a governance system
should treat "health," "medical," or "diagnosis"-adjacent requests as a
distinct, higher-sensitivity class rather than folding them into generic
PII handling.

gdpr_prototype::7.text:
Article 12-14 — Transparency and the right to be informed
----------------------------------------------------------------
Articles 12 through 14 require that information provided to data subjects
about how their personal data is processed be concise, transparent,
intelligible, and in plain language -- not buried in dense legal text.
Article 13 covers information to give when data is collected directly
from the subject (identity of the controller, purposes, legal basis,
recipients, retention period, and the subject's rights); Article 14
covers the same when data is obtained from a third party rather than the
subject directly. For an AI system, this principle extends naturally to
disclosure that an automated or AI-assisted process is involved at all --
a user interacting with an AI-driven s

gdpr_prototype::8.text:
ally to
disclosure that an automated or AI-assisted process is involved at all --
a user interacting with an AI-driven support or HR assistant has a
reasonable expectation of knowing that, which is also where GDPR's
transparency principle and the EU AI Act's Article 50 disclosure
obligation (see the EU AI Act corpus document) reinforce one another
rather than operating as two unrelated regimes.

gdpr_prototype::9.text:
Article 15 — Right of access
----------------------------------------------------------------
A data subject has the right to obtain confirmation of whether their
personal data is being processed, and if so, to access that data along
with supplementary information: the purposes of processing, the
categories of data involved, who it has been or will be disclosed to, the
retention period, and the source of the data if not collected directly
from them. In practice, this means an organization must be able to
locate and export everything a system holds about a specific person on
request, within one month (extendable to three for complex requests). An
AI governance platform that logs prompts, responses, and decisions
touching a specific individual's data should be structured so those
records can

gdpr_prototype::10.text:
t logs prompts, responses, and decisions
touching a specific individual's data should be structured so those
records can actually be retrieved by subject identity, not just by
request ID -- otherwise responding to an Article 15 request becomes a
manual, ad hoc search.

gdpr_prototype::11.text:
Article 17 — Right to erasure ("right to be forgotten")
----------------------------------------------------------------
A data subject can require a controller to erase their personal data
without undue delay where, among other grounds, the data is no longer
necessary for the purpose it was collected for, consent is withdrawn and
there is no other legal basis, the data was unlawfully processed, or the
subject objects and there are no overriding legitimate grounds. This
right is not absolute -- it does not apply where processing is necessary
for compliance with a legal obligation, for the exercise or defense of
legal claims, or for other specified exceptions. For a system like
ControlPlane, this has a direct operational consequence: audit logs
retained for compliance/accountability purpose

gdpr_prototype::12.text:
like
ControlPlane, this has a direct operational consequence: audit logs
retained for compliance/accountability purposes generally fall under a
legal-obligation exception and are not simply deleted on request, but any
underlying personal data an AI application itself stored outside that
compliance record (for example, in a vector store or cache) is squarely
within scope of an erasure request and must be locatable and removable.

gdpr_prototype::13.text:
Article 22 — Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
----------------------------------------------------------------
Article 22 gives individuals the right not to be subject to a decision
based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces
legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them --
for example, an automated rejection of a credit or loan application, or
an automated hiring decision, with no meaningful human involvement.
Exceptions apply where the decision is necessary for a contract, is
authorised by law with suitable safeguards, or is based on explicit
consent; even then, the data subject retains rights to obtain human
intervention, to express their point of view, and to contest the
decision. This is the direct regulato

gdpr_prototype::14.text:
s to obtain human
intervention, to express their point of view, and to contest the
decision. This is the direct regulatory basis for keeping a genuine
human-in-the-loop review path for high-impact automated decisions (loan
approvals, hiring recommendations) rather than allowing an AI system to
be the sole, unreviewable decision-maker in those categories -- which is
exactly the role of ControlPlane's HUMAN_REVIEW decision path for
applications tagged as high-impact (loan-decision, hiring-decision).

gdpr_prototype::15.text:
Article 25 — Data protection by design and by default
----------------------------------------------------------------
Controllers must implement appropriate technical and organizational
measures -- such as pseudonymisation -- designed to embed data protection
principles into processing from the outset ("by design"), and must
ensure that, by default, only personal data actually necessary for each
specific purpose is processed, in terms of the amount collected, the
extent of processing, the storage period, and accessibility. A governance
gateway that sits in front of every AI request is itself a natural
enforcement point for "by default" data minimisation -- for example,
redacting or withholding fields an application does not need for its
stated purpose before a response is returned, rather

gdpr_prototype::16.text:
edacting or withholding fields an application does not need for its
stated purpose before a response is returned, rather than relying on each
individual AI application to self-regulate what it surfaces.

gdpr_prototype::17.text:
Article 30 — Records of processing activities
----------------------------------------------------------------
Controllers (and processors) above certain thresholds, or engaged in
higher-risk processing, must maintain a written record of processing
activities: purposes, categories of data subjects and personal data,
categories of recipients, any international transfers, retention
schedules, and a general description of security measures. An AI
governance audit log that captures, for every governed request, the
application, department, data classification, decision, and matched
policy rule is functionally a live, continuously-updated Article 30
record for the AI systems it covers -- a byproduct of good governance
logging rather than a separate compliance exercise.

gdpr_prototype::18.text:
ecord for the AI systems it covers -- a byproduct of good governance
logging rather than a separate compliance exercise.

Article 32 — Security of processing
----------------------------------------------------------------
Controllers and processors must implement technical and organizational
measures appropriate to the risk, including (as relevant) pseudonymisation
and encryption, the ability to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity,
availability, and resilience of processing systems, the ability to
restore availability after an incident, and a process for regularly
testing and evaluating the effectiveness of these measures. HMAC-based
fingerprinting of identifiers in an audit trail (rather than storing raw
identifiers) and encryption of data at rest and in transit are concrete,
recognizable instances of "appropriate technical measures" under this
article, not just general security hygiene.

gdpr_prototype::19.text:
Articles 33-34 — Personal data breach notification
----------------------------------------------------------------
Article 33 requires a controller to notify the relevant supervisory
authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and, where
feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of it, unless the breach is
unlikely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and freedoms. Article
34 requires notifying the affected individuals directly, without undue
delay, where the breach is likely to result in a HIGH risk to their
rights and freedoms. For an AI governance platform, an incident in which
an AI application's response leaked PII it should not have surfaced --
particularly if the leak was not caught and blocked -- is exactly the
kind of event this notification clock is designed

gdpr_prototype::20.text:
particularly if the leak was not caught and blocked -- is exactly the
kind of event this notification clock is designed for, which is part of
why blocking or redacting a detected PII leak before it reaches the
requester, rather than only logging it afterward, materially changes the
organization's regulatory exposure.

gdpr_prototype::21.text:
Article 35 — Data protection impact assessment (DPIA)
----------------------------------------------------------------
Where a type of processing, in particular using new technologies, is
likely to result in a high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, the
controller must carry out a DPIA before the processing begins -- assessing
necessity and proportionality, the risks involved, and the measures
envisaged to address them. Systematic and extensive automated decision-
making with legal or similarly significant effects, and large-scale
processing of special category data, are both explicitly called out as
triggering circumstances. Deploying a new AI application into a
high-impact use case (loan decisions, hiring, health-adjacent support)
is a natural trigger point for a DPIA, and the gov

gdpr_prototype::22.text:
igh-impact use case (loan decisions, hiring, health-adjacent support)
is a natural trigger point for a DPIA, and the governance policy
configuration for that application (risk tolerance, required review
paths, data classification handling) is a natural input to, and partial
record of, that assessment.

gdpr_prototype::23.text:
Chapter V — International transfers
----------------------------------------------------------------
Personal data may only be transferred outside the European Economic Area
where the destination ensures an adequate level of protection -- either
through a formal European Commission adequacy decision for that country,
or through appropriate safeguards such as Standard Contractual Clauses or
Binding Corporate Rules. For an AI governance system, this matters most
concretely when the underlying foundation model is consumed via an
API hosted outside the EEA: the data-flow question is not only "is this
request authorized" but "where does this request, and any logged context
derived from it, actually leave to," which is a distinct dimension from
the content-based risk checks (PII, bias, hallucina

gdpr_prototype::24.text:
ived from it, actually leave to," which is a distinct dimension from
the content-based risk checks (PII, bias, hallucination) most of this
system's other controls focus on.

gdpr_prototype::25.text:
Articles 82-83 — Liability and administrative fines
----------------------------------------------------------------
Article 82 gives any person who has suffered material or non-material
damage as a result of a GDPR infringement the right to compensation from
the controller or processor involved. Article 83 sets out administrative
fines on a two-tier structure: up to EUR 10 million or 2% of total
worldwide annual turnover (whichever is higher) for certain categories of
infringement, and up to EUR 20 million or 4% of total worldwide annual
turnover (whichever is higher) for the more serious categories, including
violations of the core processing principles in Article 5, the lawful-
basis requirements of Article 6, and data subjects' rights. These figures
are the regulatory backdrop that mak

gdpr_prototype::26.text:
e lawful-
basis requirements of Article 6, and data subjects' rights. These figures
are the regulatory backdrop that makes "the AI response should not
surface unauthorized personal data" a board-level financial risk
question, not only a product-quality one.

HIPAA — Prototype Healthcare Privacy Corpus (Summary Form)
============================================================
NOTE: Plain-language summary of HIPAA's core concepts for Policy RAG
demo/retrieval purposes, not verbatim regulatory text (45 CFR Parts 160
and 164). Not legal advice.

hipaa_prototype::1.text:
cepts for Policy RAG
demo/retrieval purposes, not verbatim regulatory text (45 CFR Parts 160
and 164). Not legal advice.

Protected Health Information (PHI)
----------------------------------------------------------------
HIPAA's Privacy Rule protects "individually identifiable health
information" held by a covered entity or its business associates --
information relating to a person's past, present, or future physical or
mental health condition, the provision of health care to them, or payment
for that care, when it identifies (or could reasonably identify) the
individual. This includes obvious fields like diagnoses and prescriptions,
but also identifiers such as names, dates, and account numbers when
combined with health context.

hipaa_prototype::2.text:
Covered entities and business associates
----------------------------------------------------------------
HIPAA's obligations apply directly to "covered entities" -- health plans,
healthcare clearinghouses, and healthcare providers who transmit health
information electronically in connection with certain transactions -- and
extend to their "business associates," meaning any person or organization
that performs a function involving the use or disclosure of PHI on a
covered entity's behalf (billing services, cloud hosting, and
increasingly, AI/analytics vendors). A business associate must operate
under a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with the covered entity,
contractually obligating it to safeguard PHI to the same standard.
Most general-purpose enterprise AI copilots are not themselves

hipaa_prototype::3.text:
lly obligating it to safeguard PHI to the same standard.
Most general-purpose enterprise AI copilots are not themselves covered
entities, but if such a system processes PHI on behalf of a healthcare
organization that is a covered entity, the vendor operating it becomes a
business associate and inherits the same compliance obligations --
including, critically, that the underlying foundation-model API provider
may itself need a BAA in place before health-adjacent prompts can be sent
to it at all.

hipaa_prototype::4.text:
Minimum necessary standard
----------------------------------------------------------------
Covered entities must make reasonable efforts to limit use, disclosure,
and requests for PHI to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended
purpose. This is the healthcare-specific analogue of GDPR's data
minimisation principle (Article 5) and is directly relevant to any AI
system that could retrieve health-adjacent information in response to a
broad query -- the system should surface only what the specific,
legitimate purpose requires, not the full record.

hipaa_prototype::5.text:
to a
broad query -- the system should surface only what the specific,
legitimate purpose requires, not the full record.

Permitted disclosures without authorization
----------------------------------------------------------------
PHI may generally be used or disclosed without specific patient
authorization for treatment, payment, and healthcare operations, and in a
limited set of other circumstances (e.g. required by law, public health
activities). Disclosure for purposes outside these categories -- for
example, an internal AI assistant surfacing a colleague's health
information to someone without a treatment, payment, or operations reason
to see it -- would fall outside permitted use and should be treated as an
unauthorized-access case, structurally identical to how ControlPlane
already treats unauthorized salary or financial-record access.

hipaa_prototype::6.text:
The Security Rule — administrative, physical, and technical safeguards
----------------------------------------------------------------
Distinct from the Privacy Rule's use-and-disclosure focus, the Security
Rule specifically governs electronic PHI (ePHI) and requires three
categories of safeguard. Administrative safeguards include a designated
security official, workforce training, and periodic risk assessments.
Physical safeguards cover facility access controls and device/media
disposal. Technical safeguards -- the category most relevant to an AI
governance platform -- require access controls limiting ePHI access to
authorized users (role-based access is the standard mechanism), audit
controls that record and examine activity in systems containing ePHI,
integrity controls to prevent impr

hipaa_prototype::7.text:
chanism), audit
controls that record and examine activity in systems containing ePHI,
integrity controls to prevent improper alteration or destruction, and
transmission security to guard against unauthorized access to ePHI in
transit, typically through encryption. An audit trail that logs every
governed request touching health-classified data, with tamper-evident
fingerprinting, is a direct instance of the Security Rule's audit-controls
requirement, not a general best practice adopted independently of it.

hipaa_prototype::8.text:
Breach Notification Rule
----------------------------------------------------------------
Following a breach of unsecured PHI, a covered entity must notify
affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days
after discovery, and must notify the Department of Health and Human
Services -- immediately for breaches affecting 500 or more individuals,
or on an annual log basis for smaller breaches. Business associates must
notify the covered entity of a breach they discover, again without
unreasonable delay. An AI response that surfaces PHI to an unauthorized
requester, if not caught and blocked before the response reaches the
requester, can itself constitute a reportable breach depending on the
risk assessment required under this rule -- which is a direct argument
for bloc

hipaa_prototype::9.text:
ute a reportable breach depending on the
risk assessment required under this rule -- which is a direct argument
for blocking or redacting a detected health-data exposure pre-response,
the same logic that applies to the GDPR Article 33/34 breach-notification
clock for PII more broadly.

hipaa_prototype::10.text:
Patient rights — access, amendment, and accounting of disclosures
----------------------------------------------------------------
Individuals have the right to inspect and obtain a copy of their own PHI
held in a covered entity's "designated record set" (generally within 30
days of request), to request amendment of PHI they believe is inaccurate
or incomplete, and to receive an accounting of certain disclosures made
of their PHI over the preceding six years. As with GDPR's Article 15
right of access, this creates an operational requirement that health-
adjacent records -- including any logged AI interactions that reference a
specific patient or employee's health information -- be retrievable by
subject identity, not only by request or session ID.

hipaa_prototype::11.text:
cific patient or employee's health information -- be retrievable by
subject identity, not only by request or session ID.

Why this matters for a general-purpose enterprise copilot
----------------------------------------------------------------
Most enterprise AI copilots are not built for clinical use and are not
"covered entities" in the formal HIPAA sense, but an internal support or
HR assistant can still be asked questions that touch employee
health-related information (medical leave reasons, accommodation
requests, insurance claims). Treating any health-adjacent request as
high-sensitivity by default -- rather than only responding to explicit
"HIPAA" framing -- is the safer default posture, and mirrors GDPR Article
9's treatment of health data as a special category requiring a specific
justification rather than ordinary-course access.

hipaa_prototype::12.text:
Enforcement and penalties
----------------------------------------------------------------
HIPAA is enforced primarily by the HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR),
which can impose civil monetary penalties on a four-tier structure based
on the covered entity's or business associate's level of culpability --
ranging from cases where the entity did not know and could not reasonably
have known of the violation, up to cases of wilful neglect that are not
corrected, with per-violation-category annual caps reaching into the
millions of dollars. Criminal penalties, prosecuted by the Department of
Justice, apply to knowing violations and can include imprisonment,
particularly where PHI is obtained or disclosed under false pretenses or
with intent to sell or use it for commercial advantage or maliciou

hipaa_prototype::13.text:
PHI is obtained or disclosed under false pretenses or
with intent to sell or use it for commercial advantage or malicious harm.
As with GDPR's fine structure, the practical effect for an enterprise is
that "did the AI system disclose health information it shouldn't have"
is a question with direct financial and, in the more serious cases,
personal-liability consequences -- not only a reputational one.

policy::agent_tools.text:
Policy document: agent_tools (version 1, policy set 'agent_tools').
Scope: applies to applications ['agent_tools'] in departments [].
Default action when no rule matches: ALLOW.

Policy rule 'refund-hard-cap-block' (policy set: agent_tools, priority 100).  When amount > 2000, the resulting action is BLOCK. Reason given: Refund exceeds the maximum single-transaction limit for agent-initiated refunds; route through the manual finance workflow instead.
Policy rule 'refund-manager-signoff' (policy set: agent_tools, priority 90).  When amount > 500, the resulting action is HUMAN_REVIEW. Reason given: Refunds above $500 require manager sign-off before they execute.
Policy rule 'admin-delete-authorized' (policy set: agent_tools, priority 120).  When role == 'admin', the resulting action is ALLOW. Reason given: Admins are authorized to delete records, including PII-flagged ones, as part of normal data-lifecycle operations.
Policy rule 'delete-record-intern-hard-block' (policy set: agent_tools, priority 110).  When record_contains_pii and role == 'intern', the resulting action is BLOCK. Reason given: Interns may never delete PII-flagged records, even with a human in the loop.
Policy rule 'delete-customer-record-non-admin' (policy set: agent_tools, priority 100).  When record_contains_pii and role != 'admin', the resulting action is HUMAN_REVIEW. Reason given: Deleting a record flagged as containing PII requires admin approval.
Policy rule 'email-external-pii-block' (policy set: agent_tools, priority 100).  When is_external_recipient and contains_pii, the resulting action is BLOCK. Reason given: Refusing to send a message containing PII-pattern content to an external domain.
Policy rule 'session-carryover-escalation' (policy set: agent_tools, priority 95).  When session_risk > 0.6, the resulting action is HUMAN_REVIEW. Reason given: This session already carries elevated risk from earlier turns (e.g. a flagged multi-turn probe); escalating out of caution even though this specific call looks ordinary.

policy::finance.text:
Policy document: finance-governance (version 2, policy set 'finance').
Scope: applies to applications ['loan-decision'] in departments ['Finance'].
Default action when no rule matches: ALLOW.

Policy rule 'finance-restricted-data' (policy set: finance, priority 90). Restricted data in a high-impact finance application requires human review. When the application is one of: loan-decision and the data classification is one of: HIGH, RESTRICTED, the resulting action is HUMAN_REVIEW. Reason given: Restricted financial data requires human review.
Policy rule 'finance-pii-redact' (policy set: finance, priority 60). Redact PII in finance responses. When the pii detector score is at least 0.3, the resulting action is MODIFY. Reason given: Redact PII from financial data.
Policy rule 'finance-high-risk' (policy set: finance, priority 50). High risk finance interactions need review. When the overall risk score is at least 0.7, the resulting action is HUMAN_REVIEW. Reason given: High risk in financial context.

policy::global.text:
Policy document: global-governance (version 2, policy set 'global').
Scope: applies globally, to every application and department not covered by a more specific policy.
Default action when no rule matches: ALLOW.

Policy rule 'block-prompt-injection' (policy set: global, priority 95). High-confidence instruction-override, extraction, jailbreak, or role-manipulation attempt. When the injection detector score is at least 0.85, the resulting action is BLOCK. Reason given: High-confidence instruction-override, extraction, jailbreak, or role-manipulation attempt.
Policy rule 'block-dangerous-content' (policy set: global, priority 95). Critical unsafe-content request detected in the hot path. When the safety detector score is at least 0.8, the resulting action is BLOCK. Reason given: Critical unsafe-content request detected in the hot path.
Policy rule 'block-unauthorized-access' (policy set: global, priority 90). Block any attempt to access sensitive data without proper authorization. When the authorization detector score is at least 0.5, the resulting action is BLOCK. Reason given: Block any attempt to access sensitive data without proper authorization.
Policy rule 'block-unauthorized-pii' (policy set: global, priority 85). Block when both PII and unauthorized access are detected. When the pii detector score is at least 0.3 and the authorization detector score is at least 0.5, the resulting action is BLOCK. Reason given: Block when both PII and unauthorized access are detected.
Policy rule 'risk-based-review' (policy set: global, priority 40). High combined risk requires a human decision. When the overall risk score is at least 0.75, the resulting action is HUMAN_REVIEW. Reason given: High combined risk requires a human decision.
Policy rule 'risk-based-modification' (policy set: global, priority 30). Moderate combined risk is handled by sanitization and a controlled response. When the overall risk score is at least 0.25, the resulting action is MODIFY. Reason given: Moderate combined risk is handled by sanitization and a controlled response.

policy::hallucination_bias_rules.text:
Policy document: hallucination_bias_rules (version 1, policy set 'hallucination_bias_rules').
Scope: applies to applications ['hallucination_bias'] in departments [].
Default action when no rule matches: ALLOW.

Policy rule 'global-hallucination-high-risk' (policy set: hallucination_bias_rules, priority 0).  When signal = hallucination.hallucination_score and operator = >= and value = 0.7, the resulting action is HUMAN_REVIEW. Reason given: High hallucination risk: response contains claims the grounding engine could not verify.
Policy rule 'global-hallucination-medium-risk' (policy set: hallucination_bias_rules, priority 0).  When signal = hallucination.hallucination_score and operator = >= and value = 0.4, the resulting action is MODIFY. Reason given: Moderate hallucination risk -- response allowed through but flagged to the end user.
Policy rule 'global-bias-causal-pattern' (policy set: hallucination_bias_rules, priority 0).  When detector = bias_fast and label = protected_attribute_cited_in_decision, the resulting action is BLOCK. Reason given: Protected attribute cited as an explicit basis for a covered decision (ECOA / Title VII / EU AI Act exposure).
Policy rule 'global-bias-async-high-risk' (policy set: hallucination_bias_rules, priority 0).  When signal = fairness.bias_score and operator = >= and value = 0.6, the resulting action is HUMAN_REVIEW. Reason given: High bias risk from the counterfactual probe or LLM-judge rubric.
Policy rule 'finance-loan-decision-counterfactual-required' (policy set: hallucination_bias_rules, priority 0).  When use_case_tag = loan_decision and app_criticality = high, the resulting action is GOVERN. Reason given: Loan/credit decisions must run the counterfactual fairness probe -- direct ECOA / Fair Housing Act exposure.
Policy rule 'finance-hallucination-stricter-threshold' (policy set: hallucination_bias_rules, priority 0).  When signal = hallucination.hallucination_score and operator = >= and value = 0.3, the resulting action is HUMAN_REVIEW. Reason given: Financial decision-support has a lower hallucination tolerance than the global default (0.3 vs 0.4).
Policy rule 'hr-copilot-hallucination-employee-data' (policy set: hallucination_bias_rules, priority 0).  When signal = hallucination.hallucination_score and operator = >= and value = 0.5 and data_classification = HIGH, the resulting action is BLOCK. Reason given: Unverifiable claims about employee-identifiable data are blocked outright, not just flagged, given downstream HR/legal use.
